original_value: While increasingly deep networks are still in general desired for achieving state-of-the-art performance, for many specific inputs a simpler network might already suffice. Existing works exploited this observation by learning to skip convolutional layers in an input-dependent manner. However, we argue their binary decision scheme, i.e., either fully executing or completely bypassing one layer for a specific input, can be enhanced by introducing finer-grained, “softer” decisions. We therefore propose a Dynamic Fractional Skipping (DFS) framework. The core idea of DFS is to hypothesize layer-wise quantization (to different bitwidths) as intermediate “soft” choices to be made between fully utilizing and skipping a layer. For each input, DFS dynamically assigns a bitwidth to both weights and activations of each layer, where fully executing and skipping could be viewed as two “extremes” (i.e., full bitwidth and zero bitwidth). In this way, DFS can “fractionally” exploit a layer's expressive power during input-adaptive inference, enabling finer-grained accuracy-computational cost trade-offs. It presents a unified view to link input-adaptive layer skipping and input-adaptive hybrid quantization. Extensive experimental results demonstrate the superior tradeoff between computational cost and model expressive power (accuracy) achieved by DFS. More visualizations also indicate a smooth and consistent transition in the DFS behaviors, especially the learned choices between layer skipping and different quantizations when the total computational budgets vary, validating our hypothesis that layer quantization could be viewed as intermediate variants of layer skipping. Our source code and supplementary material are available at https://github.com/Torment123/DFS.

result.paraphrase: Although deeper networks are generally preferred for state-of-the-art performance, many individual inputs can already be handled by a simpler model. Prior work took advantage of this by learning to skip convolutional layers in an input-dependent way. We contend, however, that their binary choice—either execute a layer in full or bypass it entirely for a given input—can be improved with finer-grained, softer decisions. To that end, we introduce a Dynamic Fractional Skipping (DFS) framework. DFS is based on the idea that layer-wise quantization at different bitwidths can serve as intermediate soft options between fully using a layer and skipping it. For each input, DFS dynamically selects a bitwidth for both the weights and activations of every layer, with full execution and skipping as the two extremes, corresponding to full bitwidth and zero bitwidth. This allows DFS to fractionally use a layer’s expressive capacity during input-adaptive inference, yielding more fine-grained trade-offs between accuracy and computational cost. It offers a unified perspective that connects input-adaptive layer skipping with input-adaptive hybrid quantization. Extensive experiments show that DFS achieves a superior balance between computational cost and model expressiveness (accuracy). Additional visualizations also reveal a smooth, consistent transition in DFS behavior, particularly in the learned choices among layer skipping and different quantizations as the overall computational budget changes, supporting our hypothesis that layer quantization can be viewed as an intermediate form of layer skipping. Our source code and supplementary material are available at https://github.com/Torment123/DFS.
